12-089.r: Unemployment → loss of income, so people near the poverty line fall below it; more people below poverty line means more poverty.

12-090.r: Highest level of educated unemployment in India → Kerala (people cannot find jobs matching their qualifications).

12-091.r: Educated unemployment rises with high growth when professional or skilled education is lacking; book: A and R true, R explains A.

12-092.r: Statement: unemployment allowance for all unemployed youth above 18 → only assumption I (youth need monetary support) follows; enough government funds is not implied.

12-093.r: Roots of urban poverty lie in rural areas: low rural education → migrants get poor urban jobs and stay poor; A and R true, R explains A.

12-094.r: Employed urban males per thousand, 1999-2000 (descending) → West Bengal, Assam, Nagaland, Meghalaya; same order in PLFS 2022-23 male LFPR.
12-094.h: W-A-N-M: West Bengal > Assam > Nagaland > Meghalaya.

12-095.r: Organised sector employment growth declined in 1994-2007: from 1.2% a year (1983-94) to –0.03% a year (Economic Survey 2009-10).

12-096.r: Most unemployment in India → Structural: mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs, due to poor education and training.

12-097.r: Disguised (hidden) unemployment → marginal productivity of labour is zero; more persons employed in a job than needed, so removing them does not cut output.
12-097.h: Disguised = in disguise: looks employed, adds nothing (marginal product zero).

12-100.r: Disguised unemployment in India → mainly in the primary sector (agriculture and allied), due to heavy population pressure on land.

12-102.r: Disguised unemployment in India → mainly agricultural sector in rural areas (I and II), not manufacturing or urban areas.

12-103.r: Unemployed for a major part of the year → Usual Status unemployment (reference period 365 days, NSSO, now NSO); captures long-term open unemployment.

12-104.r: NSSO unemployment measures: Usual Principal Status (one year), Current Weekly Status (one week), Current Daily Status (each day of the week); no 'Current Monthly Status'.

12-105.r: Unemployment data in India → collected and published by NSSO (Employment-Unemployment Surveys); NSSO merged with CSO to form NSO in 2019.

12-106.r: Lowest employment elasticity → agriculture/mixed farming (0.04, 1999-2000 to 2009-2010); construction highest (1.13); finance 0.66; manufacturing 0.09.

12-107.r: Causes of unemployment → rapid population growth, lack of skill, lack of manpower planning; growth of per capita income is not a cause.

12-108.r: Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) → % of persons in the labour force (working, or seeking/available for work) in the working-age population.

12-109.r: Female LFPR fell (31.1% in 2013-2014 to 23.3% in 2017-18) due to rising education of young women and rising household income; A and R true, R explains A.

12-110.r: NSS 68th round (2011-12) unemployment rate: Current Daily Status 5.6%, Current Weekly Status 3.7%, Usual Status 2.7%.
12-110.h: Daily > Weekly > Usual: the shorter the reference period, the higher the rate here.

12-111.r: NSS 61st round → CDS unemployment about 8% in both rural (8.3%) and urban (8.2%) areas; 68th round (2011-12) → 5.6% all-India.

13-001.r: Rules of Origin → criteria to fix a product's national source; they matter because duties and restrictions depend on import source; used for customs, trade statistics, MFN/preferential treatment.

13-002.r: Supply Chain Resilience Initiative (SCRI) → launched 27 April 2021 by India, Japan and Australia (three, not five countries); ensures uninterrupted imports by diversifying suppliers.

13-003.r: India's Foreign Trade Policy → Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

13-004.r: Foreign Trade Policy 2015-20 vision → make India a major player in world trade by 2020; FTP 2023 targets US$ 2 trillion exports by 2030.

13-005.r: India (Economic Survey 2022-23): merchandise exports < imports; services exports > imports; overall current account deficit; imports of iron and steel, fertilisers, machinery increased.

13-006.r: India's total external merchandise trade in 2011-12 → Rs. 3811360 crore (Department of Commerce), so none of the given options is correct.

13-008.r: India's Trade-to-GDP ratio (World Bank): above 50% since 2000 only in 2008 and 2011-2013; 45.69% in 2007; 40% in 2019 vs 44% in 2018; no option correct.

13-009.r: India's merchandise trade as % of GDP rose from 29.5% (2004-05) to about 40.6% (2012-13); World Bank: 31.1% in 2023.

13-010.r: Exports + imports of goods: 14.2% of GDP in 1990-91 → almost three times that by 2011-12.

13-011.r: India's exports of goods and services in 2010-11 → about 22% of GDP; World Bank 2023: exports 21.9%, imports 24% of GDP.

13-012.r: India's share in global goods exports → 1.8% (2021, 2022), not 3.2%; PLI scheme (incentive on incremental sales) used by local and foreign firms; Statement-I false, II true.
hi: Production Linked Incentive (उत्पादन से जुड़ा प्रोत्साहन)

13-013.r: India's share in world exports: 1.85% in 1950, down to about 0.5-0.7% in the 1990s (answer 0.60%); 1.8% in 2022 (WTO).

13-014.r: India's share in world merchandise exports: 1.7% in 2013, 2018 and 2019; 1.6% in 2020; 1.8% in 2021 and 2022.

13-016.r: India in commercial services exports: 8th in 2014 (US$ 155.6 billion, Economic Survey 2015-16); 7th in 2022 with 4.4% share (WTO).

13-017.r: Largest share in international trade now → China (14.4% of world merchandise exports, 2022); USA led in the question period and is the largest importer.

13-018.r: India's largest trade partner region → Asia and ASEAN; Asian countries supply more than 50% of India's imports (60.92% in 2023-24).

13-022.r: In the question period India's largest import trade was with OPEC; now Asia supplies 60.92% of India's imports (2023-24).

13-023.r: 2010-11 and 2011-12 → China and UAE together had the largest share in India's trade; 2023-24 → China, USA, UAE.

13-024.r: India's largest trading partner: USA in 2006-07 (9.8%) and in 2021-22, 2022-23; China took the top spot in 2023-24, then USA, UAE.

13-025.r: India's top trading partner: USA in 2019-20, 2021-22 and 2022-23 (China 2nd, UAE 3rd); China became largest in 2023-24.
13-025.t: The answer depends on the year asked: USA for 2019-20 to 2022-23, China for 2023-24.

13-028.r: India's largest trade surplus → with USA (2019-20 to 2022-23; about US$ 36.74 billion); USA is one of the few countries India has a surplus with.

13-029.r: India's largest current account trade (goods + services) → with USA.

13-030.r: Largest source of India's imports → China (15.06% in 2023-24), then Russia and UAE.

13-032.r: South Asia trade: Indo-Sri Lanka trade fluctuated (no steady rise); textiles about 30% of India-Bangladesh trade; Bangladesh, not Nepal, is India's largest South Asian partner.

13-033.r: USA re-emerged as India's largest import source in the early nineties (A true); India did not turn to USA for defence; Russia top arms supplier (36%, 2019-23).

13-034.r: Largest destination of India's exports now → USA (17.74% in 2023-24), then UAE, Netherlands, China; UAE led in the question period.
13-034.c: Printed answer (d) USA uses current data; the explanation says (c) UAE was correct for the question period.

13-035.r: 2009-10 → UAE accounted for the largest share of India's exports.
13-035.t: Don't mix years: UAE topped India's exports in 2009-10; USA tops at present.

13-036.r: USA's share in India's exports: about 20% in the question period (option c); 17.41% in 2022-23 and 17.74% in 2023-24.

13-037.r: India's trade balance (merchandise + services), December 2022 (provisional) → (–) 11.98 USD billion; final figure (–) 7.75 USD billion.

13-038.r: India's trade balance was negative from 1949-50 onwards, except 1972-73 (Rs. 104 crore) and 1976-77 (Rs. 68 crore), when it was positive.

13-040.r: India's trade deficit peaked at US$ 195.66 billion in 2012-13, then fell till 2016-17 as both POL and non-POL deficits declined; A and R true, R explains A.

13-041.r: Balance of Trade → difference between value of exports and imports of goods only (visible items); services and transfers are not included.

13-042.r: Net exports = Exports – Imports (goods and services); positive = trade surplus, negative = trade deficit.

13-043.r: Payment for foreign trade → recorded in the Balance of Payments (account of all international transactions of a country).

13-044.r: Balance of Payments → systematic record of all economic transactions (goods, services, assets) between residents and the rest of the world, usually for a year; current and capital accounts.

13-047.r: Balance of Payments includes visible trade (goods), invisible trade (services, transfers) and borrowings: all of the above.

13-048.r: Current Account of BoP → Balance of Trade (goods) + Balance of Invisibles (services, transfers); foreign assets and SDRs are not part of it.
13-048.h: Current account = T + I: Trade + Invisibles.

13-049.r: Current Account Deficit → payments for goods, services, transfers and net income exceed receipts; occurs when a country imports (not exports) more; A true, R false.

13-051.r: India's top import by rupee value in 2000-01 (among options) → pearls, precious and semi-precious stones, ahead of edible oils and fertilisers.

13-052.r: India spends the most foreign exchange on petroleum products (crude and products US$ 209418 million, about 29.4% of imports in 2022-23).

13-054.r: Most important item in India's imports → petroleum (crude and products 26.52% of imports in 2023-24); iron and steel 3.52%, edible oils 2.20%.

13-055.r: Two largest import items → petroleum products (fuel) and capital goods; petroleum products alone have the maximum share.
